summary: Specifies version 6 of the Internet Protocol, also called IP Next Generation or IPng. It was a standards-track document, later replaced by RFC 2460.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 is the successor to IPv4. Its main changes are bigger addresses, a smaller and simpler header, options moved into separate headers that routers can ignore, a way to mark a group of packets as a special flow, and hooks for authentication and encryption.

questions: what does the ipv6 header contain
subtitle: The specification of version 6 of the Internet Protocol: the header, extension headers, packet sizes, flow labels and priority.

tldr.problem: IP version 4 had too few addresses for the growth of the Internet, a header that every router had to work through, and little room for new features.
tldr.mechanism: IPv6 raises the address size to 128 bits, simplifies the header, moves optional information into separate extension headers that routers can skip, and adds a flow label and a priority field.
tldr.outcome: The specification defined the base of the protocol that IPv6 implementations follow. This RFC was later obsoleted by RFC 2460.

today: RFC 1883 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 2460, so read that document for the current specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IP version 6 is a new version of the Internet Protocol, designed as a successor to IP version 4. The changes fall into five categories. Expanded addressing: the address size grows from 32 bits to 128 bits, to support more levels of addressing hierarchy, a much greater number of addressable nodes and simpler auto-configuration of addresses, and a scope field is added to multicast addresses, along with a new anycast address type used to send a packet to any one of a group of nodes. Header format simplification: some IPv4 header fields are dropped or made optional, to reduce the common-case processing cost of handling a packet and the bandwidth cost of the header. Improved support for extensions and options: the way header options are encoded changes, allowing more efficient forwarding, less stringent limits on the length of options and more flexibility for introducing new options later. Flow labelling: a new capability lets a sender label packets belonging to a particular traffic flow for which it requests special handling, such as non-default quality of service or real-time service. Authentication and privacy: extensions to support authentication, data integrity and optional data confidentiality are specified for IPv6.

This document specifies the basic IPv6 header and the initially defined IPv6 extension headers and options. It also discusses packet size issues, the semantics of flow labels and priority, and the effects of IPv6 on upper-layer protocols. The format and semantics of IPv6 addresses are specified separately in RFC 1884, and the IPv6 version of ICMP, which all IPv6 implementations are required to include, is specified in RFC 1885.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 is the successor to IPv4. Its main changes are bigger addresses, a smaller and simpler header, options moved into separate headers that routers can ignore, a way to mark a group of packets as a special flow, and hooks for authentication and encryption.

sections.title: The IPv6 Header
sections.content:
The IPv6 header has a fixed layout. The first four bits hold the version number, which is 6. The next four bits hold the priority value, and the following 24 bits hold the flow label. The next two octets give the payload length, the length in octets of the rest of the packet following the IPv6 header; if it is zero, the payload length is carried in a Jumbo Payload hop-by-hop option instead. The next octet is the Next Header selector, which identifies the type of header immediately following the IPv6 header and uses the same values as the IPv4 protocol field. The last octet of the first row is the Hop Limit, an unsigned integer decremented by one by each node that forwards the packet, with the packet discarded if the limit reaches zero.

The remaining rows hold the 128-bit source address of the originator of the packet and the 128-bit destination address of the intended recipient, which is not necessarily the ultimate recipient if a Routing header is present.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPv6 header is a fixed size. It carries the version, a priority value, a flow label, the payload length, the type of the next header, a hop limit that counts down as the packet crosses routers, and the 128-bit source and destination addresses.

sections.title: Extension Headers
sections.content:
In IPv6, optional internet-layer information is encoded in separate headers that may be placed between the IPv6 header and the upper-layer header. There are a small number of these extension headers, each identified by a distinct Next Header value, and a packet may carry zero, one or more of them, each identified by the Next Header field of the preceding header.

With one exception, extension headers are not examined or processed by any node along a packet's delivery path until the packet reaches the node identified in the Destination Address field of the IPv6 header. There, demultiplexing on the Next Header field invokes the module to process the first extension header, or the upper-layer header if no extension header is present. Extension headers must be processed strictly in the order they appear in the packet, so a receiver must not, for example, scan through a packet looking for a particular kind of extension header and process it before the preceding ones. The exception is the Hop-by-Hop Options header, which carries information that must be examined and processed by every node along the delivery path, including the source and destination. It must immediately follow the IPv6 header, and its presence is indicated by the value zero in the Next Header field of the IPv6 header.

Each extension header is an integer multiple of 8 octets long, so that 8-octet alignment is retained for subsequent headers, and its multi-octet fields are aligned on their natural boundaries. A full implementation includes the Hop-by-Hop Options, Routing (Type 0), Fragment, Destination Options, Authentication and Encapsulating Security Payload headers. When more than one is used, the recommended order is the IPv6 header, Hop-by-Hop Options, Destination Options for the first destination, Routing, Fragment, Authentication, Encapsulating Security Payload, Destination Options for the final destination, and then the upper-layer header. Each extension header should occur at most once, except the Destination Options header, which should occur at most twice.
sections.plainLanguage: Anything optional in IPv6 lives in its own header placed after the main header, and the Next Header field says which one comes next. Routers normally pass these headers along without reading them, with one exception: the Hop-by-Hop Options header, which every router on the path must read.

sections.title: Packet Size and Fragmentation
sections.content:
IPv6 requires that every link on the Internet have an MTU of 576 octets or greater; a link that cannot convey a 576-octet packet in one piece must provide fragmentation and reassembly at a layer below IPv6. From each link to which a node is directly attached, the node must be able to accept packets as large as that link's MTU, and links with a configurable MTU must be configured for at least 576 octets. It is strongly recommended that IPv6 nodes implement Path MTU Discovery to discover and take advantage of paths with an MTU greater than 576 octets, though a minimal implementation may simply restrict itself to sending packets no larger than 576 octets.

To send a packet larger than a path's MTU, a node may use the IPv6 Fragment header to fragment the packet at the source and have it reassembled at the destination, but such fragmentation is discouraged in any application that is able to adjust its packets to fit the measured path MTU. A node must be able to accept a fragmented packet that, after reassembly, is as large as 1500 octets including the IPv6 header, and it must not send fragments that reassemble to a size greater than 1500 octets unless it has explicit knowledge that the destination can reassemble a packet of that size.

Reassembly rules govern the process. An original packet is reassembled only from fragments that have the same source address, destination address and fragment identification. The unfragmentable part of the reassembled packet consists of all the headers up to but not including the Fragment header of the first fragment, and the fragmentable part is built from the fragments themselves; the Fragment header does not appear in the reassembled packet. If insufficient fragments are received to complete reassembly within 60 seconds of the arrival of the first fragment, reassembly must be abandoned and all the fragments discarded, and if the first fragment was received an ICMP Time Exceeded message should be sent to its source.
sections.plainLanguage: Every IPv6 link must be able to carry at least 576-byte packets. Senders are expected to find the largest packet the path can take rather than splitting packets, because a lost fragment loses the whole packet. The receiving end puts the fragments back together, and gives up if they do not all arrive within 60 seconds.

sections.title: Flow Labels and Priority
sections.content:
The 24-bit flow label field may be used by a source to label those packets for which it requests special handling by the IPv6 routers, such as non-default quality of service or real-time service. A flow is a sequence of packets sent from a particular source to a particular destination for which the source desires special handling. There may be several active flows from a source to a destination, as well as traffic that is not associated with any flow, and a flow is uniquely identified by the combination of a source address and a non-zero flow label. Packets that do not belong to a flow carry a flow label of zero.

Flow labels are assigned by the flow's source node and must be chosen pseudo-randomly and uniformly from the range 1 to FFFFFF hex, so that any set of bits within the field can be used as a hash key by routers looking up the state associated with the flow. All packets belonging to the same flow must be sent with the same source address, destination address, priority and flow label, and with the same contents in the extension headers up to and including any Routing header. A source must not re-use a flow label for a new flow within the lifetime of any flow-handling state that might have been established for its previous use, which sets the minimum interval between the last packet of one flow and the first packet of a new flow using the same label at 6 seconds. Cached flow-handling state set up opportunistically by a router must be discarded no more than 6 seconds after it is established, and routers that do not support the flow label must set it to zero when originating a packet, pass it on unchanged when forwarding, and ignore it when receiving.

The 4-bit priority field enables a source to identify the desired delivery priority of its packets relative to other packets from the same source. Values 0 through 7 are used for traffic whose source performs congestion control and backs off in response to congestion, such as TCP traffic. Values 8 through 15 are used for traffic that does not back off, such as real-time packets sent at a constant rate, where the lowest value should be used for packets the sender is most willing to have discarded under congestion and the highest value for those it is least willing to have discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: The flow label lets a sender say that a group of its packets should be treated as one conversation, so that routers can keep state for it. The sender picks the label at random, uses the same one for every packet in the group, and waits at least 6 seconds before reusing it for a different group. The priority field says how important the packets are: 0 to 7 for traffic that slows down under congestion, 8 to 15 for traffic that does not.

sections.title: Upper-Layer Checksums and Security
sections.content:
Any transport or other upper-layer protocol that includes the addresses from the IP header in its checksum computation must be modified for use over IPv6, to include the 128-bit IPv6 addresses instead of the 32-bit IPv4 addresses. The pseudo-header used for that computation carries the source address, the destination address, the payload length, and the Next Header value that identifies the upper-layer protocol, such as 6 for TCP or 17 for UDP. Where the packet contains a Routing header, the destination address used in the pseudo-header is that of the final destination.

Unlike IPv4, the UDP checksum is not optional over IPv6: a node originating a UDP packet must compute a UDP checksum over the packet and the pseudo-header, and if the result is zero it must be changed to hex FFFF, and an IPv6 receiver must discard a UDP packet containing a zero checksum. The IPv6 version of ICMP includes the pseudo-header in its checksum computation, unlike the IPv4 version of ICMP, to protect ICMP from misdelivery or corruption of the IPv6 header fields on which it depends, which are not covered by an internet-layer checksum. The Next Header value in the pseudo-header for ICMP is 58.

The Security Considerations of the document state that it specifies that the IP Authentication Header and the IP Encapsulating Security Payload be used with IPv6, in conformance with the Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol. IPv6 nodes are also not required to enforce a maximum packet lifetime, which is why the IPv4 Time to Live field was renamed Hop Limit, and any upper-layer protocol that relies on the internet layer to limit packet lifetime ought to provide its own mechanism for discarding obsolete packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Checksums in TCP, UDP and ICMP have to change for IPv6, because the addresses they cover are now 128 bits long. The UDP checksum is no longer optional, because IPv6 has no header checksum of its own to catch a corrupted address. The RFC also requires the two IPsec headers to be available for IPv6.
